outcome: As of 12 Oct 2026 the conjecture is still open on everything I could find: since 26 Jan 2024 there are three new events (Chang and Sun's proof for the class of 4-regular planar graphs, dated 28 Oct 2024; Förster, Kobourov, Miller and Zink's grid bounds for integer-length drawings of trees and cacti, dated 4 Sep 2025; and Kintali's arXiv 'On the Harborth Conjecture, Part I', dated 17 Jun 2026, which reduces the stronger Kleber version to two unproved conjectures and proves a quadrilateral lemma), and Kintali's paper contains an AI disclosure that names no system.
problem_asks: Read as the literature reads it: (1) for every planar graph G (an infinite class, all planar graphs), (2) there is a drawing of G in the plane with straight-line edges, (3) crossing-free (so the drawing is a planar embedding), (4) in which every edge has integer length. Vertices need not be integer points; because lengths can be scaled, rational lengths are equivalent to integer lengths. The frozen statement reads 'every planar graph can be drawn with integer edge lengths' and does not say 'crossing-free' in terms; without that requirement the question is settled, since every graph has an integral drawing (MathWorld cites Müller 1953 and Harborth and Möller 1994; not opened by me), so crossing-freeness is the part being asked. Not asked by this bullet: integer vertex coordinates. That stronger variant, Kleber's conjecture (Kintali's Conjecture 1.6, 'every planar graph has an integral drawing', meaning vertices in Z² as well), is a different question, though it implies this one.

events.what_happened: J. H. J. Almering, 'Rational quadrilaterals', Indagationes Mathematicae 25 (1963) 192–199. Cited by Kintali as one of the two sources (with Berry 1992) for the known triangle case: a point inside a rational triangle whose distances to the three vertices are all rational. I did not open Almering's paper; its content is known to me only from Kintali's citation and attribution.
events.delivers: Per Kintali's attribution only: part of the rational-distance point result for triangles (the triangle case, which Kintali states as Corollary 1.17 and presents as known). A tool for a single triangle; it says nothing about any planar graph.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. This is an ingredient in the reduction, not a result on the conjecture.
events.direction: Not a result about the conjecture's direction; supports a lemma that a positive construction would need.

events.what_happened: Harborth, Kemnitz, Möller and Süssenbach, 'Ganzzahlige planare Darstellungen der platonischen Körper', Elemente der Mathematik (1987). Wikipedia credits this paper with the original publication of the conjecture, and Kemnitz and Harborth (2001) do the same. It gives plane integer-length drawings of the five Platonic solid graphs. Volume and page numbers differ across sources: Elemente der Mathematik 42 (1987) 118–122 in one reference and 45(5) 118–122 in another. I did not open the paper; the content comes from Wikipedia's summary and search snippets.
events.delivers: Integer-length, crossing-free straight-line drawings of the five Platonic graphs (tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, icosahedron). Finitely many specific graphs, all of bounded size. This is the earliest positive evidence in the line of work; it is not a case of the conjecture in the sense of an infinite family.
events.remains: Every planar graph other than these five, which is every part of problem_asks beyond the Platonic cases.

checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal; I did not verify its referee process
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (I did not open it, so I did not check the drawings)

events.directly_checkable: The five drawings are finite and could be checked by hand, but I did not see them.
events.direction: Positive, for five specific graphs; the conjecture itself is a universal claim about all planar graphs, so these instances cut in the conjectured direction without reaching it.
events.object: Explicit integer-length crossing-free drawings of each of the five Platonic graphs. Whether the drawings are explicit or come from a non-constructive argument, I did not establish; Wikipedia describes them only as showing that integral Fáry embeddings exist for all five Platonic solids.

events.what_happened: T. G. Berry, 'Points at rational distance from the vertices of a triangle', Acta Arithmetica 62 (1992), no. 4, 391–398, DOI 10.4064/aa-62-4-391-398. Kintali's reference list gives the same citation, and Kintali uses it for the triangle case. Later papers summarised by search describe Berry's result as density of points at rational distance from the three vertices of a triangle under conditions on the sides, and Geelen, Guo and McKinnon use Berry's result for the cubic case. I did not open Berry's paper.
events.delivers: Per the secondary descriptions: rational-distance points for a single triangle (a density result under side conditions). It covers triangles only. The conjecture's reduction needs such points for faces with more vertices, per Kintali's reduction to polygons with at most five vertices.
events.remains: All of problem_asks; this is a lemma-level tool, not a result on any planar graph.

checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal; I did not verify its referee process

events.direction: Supports the positive direction only as a lemma for triangles; does not bear directly on whether the conjecture holds.

events.what_happened: Harborth and Möller, on the Platonic graphs: 'Minimum Integral Drawings of the Platonic Graphs', Mathematics Magazine 67 (1994) 355–358 (per a MathWorld snippet), and 'Ebene geradlinige Darstellungen der platonischen Graphen mit wenigen verschiedenen Kantenlängen', Abhandlungen der Braunschweigischen Wissenschaftlichen Gesellschaft 45 (1994) 7–20 (per a search result). I did not open either; I could not confirm whether they are the same work or companion papers.
events.delivers: Per the snippets only: minimal integral drawings of the Platonic graphs, with the German title suggesting a count of distinct edge lengths as the optimisation. Finitely many specific graphs.
events.remains: Every planar graph outside the Platonic family.

events.what_happened: A. Kemnitz and H. Harborth, 'Plane integral drawings of planar graphs', Discrete Mathematics 236 (1–3) (2001) 191–195, DOI 10.1016/S0012-365X(00)00442-8. I did not open the paper. Secondary reports say it gives a method for maximal planar graphs (remove a low-degree vertex, triangulate, recurse, then reinsert the vertex inside its face) and a lemma that a point exists on the line through two given vertices at rational distance from four given vertices. Both are second-hand: they come from search summaries of the Chang and Sun slides and of Kintali's paper, neither of which I could read in full.
events.delivers: Per secondary reports only: a delete-and-reinsert construction for maximal planar graphs (which reduces the general problem to triangulations) and a rational-distance point lemma for four vertices. Whether it gives integer-length drawings for any class beyond maximal planar graphs, I did not establish.
events.remains: The general conjecture, and whatever the construction does not cover. If the reports are right, the construction is for maximal planar graphs only.

checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal; I did not verify its referee process

events.doubts: Only second-hand descriptions were available, so the scope claims above are unverified.
events.direction: Positive for a class (if the reports are right); does not bear on the general claim.

events.what_happened: Jim Geelen, Anjie Guo and David McKinnon, 'Straight line embeddings of cubic planar graphs with integer edge lengths', Journal of Graph Theory 58 (3) (2008) 270–274, DOI 10.1002/jgt.20304, online 10 Apr 2008 (from a search snippet; the publisher page was not opened). The abstract, as quoted in the snippet, says every simple cubic planar graph admits a planar embedding with each edge a straight segment of integer length. The Waterloo PDF I opened is a later copy (its metadata creation date is 10 Oct 2013) and its body text was not extractable. A search summary says the paper poses the all-planar-graphs question as a conjecture; I did not confirm that from the paper itself.
events.revisions: Manuscript received 5 Dec 2006, revised 16 Jan 2008 (search snippet).
events.delivers: Integer-length planar straight-line embeddings for every simple cubic planar graph (per the title and abstract). Restricted class. Some later summaries describe the class as all planar graphs of maximum degree 3, which is broader than cubic; I did not resolve which is right.
events.remains: Planar graphs that are not cubic (and, if the summaries are read as broader, planar graphs of maximum degree 4 or more).

checked_by.who: Journal of Graph Theory (journal of record)
checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal; I did not verify its referee process

events.what_happened: Cited by Wikipedia as 'Biedl (2011)'. The 2025 Förster et al. paper, as summarised by search, says Biedl shows how to draw planar max-degree-3 graphs with integer edge lengths and integer coordinates. A search summary of a later paper adds that Biedl observes the technique applies to all planar (2,1)-sparse graphs. I did not locate Biedl's paper, so its title, venue and exact statement are unconfirmed.
events.delivers: Per secondary summaries only: integer-length and integer-coordinate planar drawings of max-degree-3 planar graphs (the Kleber-type version), and possibly all planar (2,1)-sparse graphs. Not verified.
events.remains: Planar graphs outside the classes named above, and the general conjecture.
events.doubts: Source not located; the scope is taken from secondary summaries.
events.direction: Positive for classes, if the secondary summaries are right.

events.what_happened: Cited by Wikipedia and by the Chang and Sun slide summary as Benediktovich (2013). Per Wikipedia, it gives integer-length (and, for the Kleber version, integer-coordinate) drawings for planar graphs of maximum degree 4 that are not 4-regular and for planar 3-trees. I did not locate the paper, so the title, venue and statement are unconfirmed.
events.delivers: Per Wikipedia only: for the non-4-regular planar graphs of maximum degree 4 and for planar 3-trees, integer-length drawings (the Wikipedia summary places integer-coordinate results here too; a search summary instead describes Benediktovich's 2013 result as rational drawings).
events.remains: The general conjecture; the non-4-regular maximum-degree-4 class is covered only if this source is right.
events.doubts: Source not located. The two secondary descriptions disagree on whether the result is about integer coordinates or rational coordinates.
events.direction: Positive for classes, if the Wikipedia summary is right.

events.what_happened: Timothy Sun, 'Drawing some 4-regular planar graphs with integer edge lengths', Proceedings of the Canadian Conference on Computational Geometry (CCCG 2013). Wikipedia cites it, with a PDF link to cccg.ca (paper_47.pdf; I did not retrieve that PDF). Per a search summary of the 2024 Chang and Sun paper, this 2013 work covered some classes (the low-connectivity case, and the diamond and small-edge-cut cases in the 2024 abstract's terms) and contained an error in one of its constructions, which the 2024 paper corrects.
events.delivers: Per secondary summaries only: integer-length embeddings for some classes of 4-regular planar graphs, with one construction in error (corrected in 2024). Does not cover all 4-regular planar graphs.
events.remains: Every 4-regular planar graph outside the covered classes, and every other planar graph.

events.what_happened: Daniel J. Chang and Timothy Sun (both Department of Computer Science, San Francisco State University), 'Harborth's Conjecture for 4-Regular Planar Graphs', 32nd International Symposium on Graph Drawing and Network Visualization (GD 2024), LIPIcs vol. 320, pp. 38:1–38:9, DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.GD.2024.38. Abstract (opened on the Dagstuhl page), first sentence: 'We show that every 4-regular planar graph has a straight-line embedding in the plane where all edges have integer length.' The second sentence says the construction extends earlier ideas to 4-regular planar graphs with diamond subgraphs or small edge cuts. Dagstuhl gives 28 Oct 2024 as the publication date. I did not confirm the conference dates, and the first written version may predate that date; I found no arXiv version. The paper proves rational lengths, which is equivalent to integer lengths by scaling.
events.delivers: Every 4-regular planar graph admits a crossing-free straight-line drawing with every edge of integer length (the proof is for rational lengths, equivalent by scaling). The class is restricted to 4-regular graphs. The Chang and Sun slides, as summarised, say the maximum-degree-4 case is now covered in total, which would combine this result with the non-4-regular subquartic results (Benediktovich 2013 and Biedl 2011, both second-hand).
events.remains: Every planar graph that is not 4-regular. If the subquartic reports are right, what remains is planar graphs of maximum degree 5 or more that are not 4-regular, which is most of the class.

events.direction: Positive for the 4-regular class; cuts in the conjectured direction for that class. Does not settle the general conjecture.

events.what_happened: Henry Förster, Stephen Kobourov, Jacob Miller and Johannes Zink, 'Drawing Trees and Cacti with Integer Edge Lengths on a Polynomial-Size Grid', arXiv:2509.04168, submitted 4 Sep 2025 (v1, four authors, title as printed on the v1 HTML). Also a GD 2025 poster (LIPIcs vol. 357, GD2025.48). The arXiv listing I opened now shows v2 (25 Sep 2026) with a different title, 'Embedding Trees and Cactus Graphs with Integer Edge Lengths on a Compact Integer Grid', and a fifth author (Aaron Büngener). The v1 HTML I read says the paper proves Kleber-type 'truly integral' drawings (integer edge lengths and integer vertex coordinates) for trees and cacti, on grids of bounds (2π²/3)·t·d (within O(n²) per side) for trees and O(n³) for cacti, with an Ω(n) lower bound for stars in that model, and says the general conjecture is open. One search summary gives tree grids as O(n log n). I did not reconcile these; I read the v1 HTML through a summarising fetch.
events.revisions: v1 4 Sep 2025 (title 'Drawing Trees and Cacti with Integer Edge Lengths on a Polynomial-Size Grid', four authors); v2 25 Sep 2026 (title 'Embedding Trees and Cactus Graphs with Integer Edge Lengths on a Compact Integer Grid', five authors, per the current listing).
events.delivers: Trees and cacti (planar classes of a special kind) admit crossing-free straight-line drawings with integer edge lengths and integer vertex coordinates on polynomial-size grids, computable in polynomial time (linear time per the abstract summary). The result is for these two classes only.
events.remains: All planar graphs other than trees and cacti: the general Harborth conjecture (integer edge lengths) and the general Kleber conjecture. The authors list the general question as open, per the v1 HTML.

events.doubts: Grid-size bounds disagree between the v1 HTML reading (O(n²) for trees) and a search summary (O(n log n) for trees). Read the paper before relying on either figure.
events.direction: Positive for trees and cacti, cutting in the conjectured direction only for those classes; the paper says the general conjecture is open.

events.what_happened: Shiva Kintali (sole author, email address only, no affiliation shown), 'On the Harborth Conjecture. Part I', arXiv:2607.02535 (math.CO). v1 submitted Wed 17 Jun 2026, 22:49:31 UTC; v2 revised 13 Jul 2026 (both from the arXiv abstract page). The HTML of v2 states on its first page 'dated June 1st 2026', which does not match the arXiv v1 date; I have kept the arXiv date. The paper states Harborth's conjecture as 'Conjecture 1.5: every planar graph has a plane straight-line drawing whose edge lengths are integers' and Kleber's as 'Conjecture 1.6: every planar graph has an integral drawing' (vertices in Z²). Main results, as read from the v2 HTML: Theorem 1.25, assuming Conjectures 1.21 (quadrilateral diagonal insertion) and 1.24 (pentagon kernel insertion), every planar graph has an integral drawing; Theorem 1.26, for every simple non-degenerate quadrilateral (no three vertices collinear, convex or concave) with integer vertex coordinates, integer side lengths and an integer-length interior diagonal UV, there is a rational point on the open segment UV whose four distances to the vertices are rational. The triangle case is stated as Corollary 1.17 and credited to Almering and Berry. The paper says later parts will treat non-degenerate pentagons and then degenerate quadrilaterals and pentagons.
events.revisions: v1 17 Jun 2026; v2 13 Jul 2026 (arXiv abstract page). The AI-use statements below appear in the v2 HTML; my extraction of the v1 HTML found no such statement, but I could not confirm the full v1 text, so I cannot say whether they were added in v2. The v1 and v2 appendices also differ in title.
events.delivers: Conditional: if Conjectures 1.21 and 1.24 hold, every planar graph has an integral drawing (vertices in Z² and integer edge lengths), which implies integer edge lengths and so Harborth's conjecture. Unconditional: the quadrilateral lemma (Theorem 1.26) for non-degenerate quadrilaterals with the stated integrality hypotheses, which gives a rational point with rational distances to all four vertices on the interior integer diagonal. The paper does not prove the pentagon statement or the degenerate cases. It does not prove Harborth's conjecture or Kleber's conjecture unconditionally.
events.remains: Unconditionally: Harborth's conjecture and Kleber's conjecture, for all planar graphs. Also open in the paper: Conjecture 1.21 (quadrilateral diagonal insertion) and Conjecture 1.24 (pentagon kernel insertion), which the reduction assumes; non-degenerate pentagons; degenerate quadrilaterals; degenerate pentagons. The paper's own list places the last three in later parts.
events.time_since_posted: About 4 months since v1 (17 Jun 2026) as of 12 Oct 2026; about 3 months since v2 (13 Jul 2026). I found no public engagement, citation, or review in searches.
events.directly_checkable: The quadrilateral theorem is an existence claim (a rational point with rational distances), not an explicit configuration I could see. The paper cites LMFDB and Cremona tables for rank and torsion of specific elliptic curves in the proof; that is data lookup, not a machine-checked proof.
events.doubts: (i) The reduction is conditional on Conjectures 1.21 and 1.24, which the paper does not prove. (ii) The v2 AI-use statements say: 'The author wrote the proofs case by case and used AI to verify the proofs and find the missing gaps.' and 'The author fixed those missing gaps and iteratively verified the proofs with AI.' This means earlier drafts had gaps that were found with AI assistance; the paper does not identify them, and does not say whether later checks found more. (iii) Single author, no affiliation, arXiv only, no venue or review found. (iv) The statement 'Some of the examples were generated by AI and verified by the author' does not say which examples. (v) The unconditional result is for non-degenerate quadrilaterals with integrality hypotheses only, and is a lemma rather than a drawing for any graph.
events.direction: Partial and conditional progress on the stronger Kleber version, which would imply Harborth's conjecture. The unconditional part is a quadrilateral lemma. The paper says it does not settle either conjecture. It cuts in the conjectured direction; there is no counterexample.

disputes.summary: Chang and Sun's slides, as summarised by search, say Harborth's conjecture is now known for all graphs of maximum degree 4. Wikipedia and Kintali describe the same result as covering 4-regular planar graphs (Chang–Sun 2024) plus non-4-regular maximum-degree-4 planar graphs (Benediktovich 2013 per Wikipedia). Together these would cover max-degree-4 graphs, but I could not read the slides or locate the Benediktovich paper, so I did not reconcile the two statements.
Harborth et al. (1987) volume: Elemente der Mathematik 42 (1987) 118–122 in Wikipedia-derived and EuDML sources, versus 45(5) 118–122 in another reference. Not resolved; I did not open the paper.

Förster et al. (arXiv 2509.04168): v1 title 'Drawing Trees and Cacti with Integer Edge Lengths on a Polynomial-Size Grid' (4 Sep 2025, four authors) versus the current listing 'Embedding Trees and Cactus Graphs with Integer Edge Lengths on a Compact Integer Grid' (v2, 25 Sep 2026, five authors). Grid-size claims also differ between the v1 HTML reading and a search summary. Not reconciled.

Kintali (arXiv 2607.02535): the v2 HTML says 'dated June 1st 2026' on its first page, but arXiv gives v1 as 17 Jun 2026. The AI-use statements are in the v2 HTML; whether they were in v1 is not established by my extraction.

summary: The conjecture remains open on every source I could read, including Wikipedia's article as fetched. The historical record gives positive results only for restricted classes: the five Platonic graphs (Harborth et al. 1987), the cubic planar graphs (Geelen, Guo and McKinnon, J. Graph Theory 2008), and some 4-regular and subquartic classes, through Sun (CCCG 2013), Benediktovich (2013) and Biedl (2011), of which the last two I could not locate. Kemnitz and Harborth (2001) is recorded from second-hand descriptions only. Three post-window events bear on it. Chang and Sun (GD 2024, LIPIcs, dated 28 Oct 2024) prove that every 4-regular planar graph has an integer-length crossing-free straight-line drawing; this is the strongest post-window result for the conjecture as stated, but it is a class result, and the Chang–Sun slides, as summarised, say maximum degree 4 is now covered in total, which would combine it with the subquartic results. Förster, Kobourov, Miller and Zink (arXiv 2509.04168, 4 Sep 2025) give polynomial-grid integer-length drawings for trees and cacti only, and say the general question is open. Kintali (arXiv 2607.02535, 17 Jun 2026; v2 13 Jul 2026) is the most consequential new source for the stronger Kleber version: Theorem 1.25 reduces that version, and so Harborth's conjecture, to two conjectures (1.21 and 1.24) which the paper does not prove, and Theorem 1.26 proves a quadrilateral lemma for non-degenerate quadrilaterals; the pentagon case and the degenerate cases are deferred to later parts that I could not find. The call that matters most for the judging pass is how far Kintali's paper goes. Its unconditional content is a lemma, its main reduction is conditional, and the author states that the proofs were checked with AI tools that found gaps, which the author then fixed. No named system and no independent checks are reported. For AI involvement: I searched for AI involvement in Harborth's conjecture, including OpenAI, Google DeepMind, AlphaEvolve and Claude/GPT/Gemini terms, and found nothing else. The OpenAI planar unit-distance disproof (May 2026) and DeepMind's Erdős problem results concern other problems. The only AI involvement found is Kintali's own disclosure, which says 'AI' with no system named: AI was used to verify proofs and find gaps, 'Some of the examples were generated by AI and verified by the author', and 'The introduction section was almost entirely written by AI and verified by the author'. Per §5.4 I have not put an entry in ai.systems, because no system is named; none_found is false because AI was involved; the verification uses are recorded as such, and the example generation is not characterised, since the paper does not say which examples. The v2 HTML contains the disclosure. My extraction of v1 found no such statement, but I could not read the full v1 text, so I did not establish when it was added.
competing_reading: On the narrow reading, Kintali's unconditional content is a single quadrilateral lemma, its main reduction is conditional on two open conjectures, and nothing in the paper is credited to an AI system as an idea; the disclosed AI use is proof checking, which §5.4 excludes from ai.systems. On the broad reading, the paper's proofs were 'written case by case' and gaps were found by AI and then fixed, and 'some of the examples were generated by AI'. If those examples supported the quadrilateral lemma, the AI contribution may be load-bearing in a sense the narrow reading misses. Separately, for Chang and Sun, the narrow reading treats the result as a 4-regular class result; the broad reading, based on the slides' claim that maximum degree 4 is now covered, would give a much larger class. I could not read the slides or the Benediktovich paper, so I cannot decide between these.
what_would_settle_it: (1) Full text of Kintali v1 and v2, checked for when the AI-use statements were added, which examples were AI-generated and whether they feed the lemma, and what the 'missing gaps' were. (2) Whether Conjectures 1.21 and 1.24 are proved elsewhere or in Part II. (3) The Chang–Sun paper's full text (acknowledgements and any AI statement) and the Chang–Sun slides, to confirm the 4-regular scope and the maximum-degree-4 claim. (4) The Benediktovich 2013 and Biedl 2011 papers, to confirm the non-4-regular subquartic and max-degree-3 scopes. (5) The Förster et al. v1 and v2 full text, to reconcile the grid bounds and the author list. (6) Any independent review or citation of Kintali, Chang–Sun or Förster et al. after the dates recorded.

event.what_happened: Daniel J. Chang and Timothy Sun (both Department of Computer Science, San Francisco State University), 'Harborth's Conjecture for 4-Regular Planar Graphs', 32nd International Symposium on Graph Drawing and Network Visualization (GD 2024), LIPIcs vol. 320, pp. 38:1–38:9, DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.GD.2024.38. Abstract (opened on the Dagstuhl page), first sentence: 'We show that every 4-regular planar graph has a straight-line embedding in the plane where all edges have integer length.' The second sentence says the construction extends earlier ideas to 4-regular planar graphs with diamond subgraphs or small edge cuts. Dagstuhl gives 28 Oct 2024 as the publication date. I did not confirm the conference dates, and the first written version may predate that date; I found no arXiv version. The paper proves rational lengths, which is equivalent to integer lengths by scaling.
event.delivers: Every 4-regular planar graph admits a crossing-free straight-line drawing with every edge of integer length (the proof is for rational lengths, equivalent by scaling). The class is restricted to 4-regular graphs. The Chang and Sun slides, as summarised, say the maximum-degree-4 case is now covered in total, which would combine this result with the non-4-regular subquartic results (Benediktovich 2013 and Biedl 2011, both second-hand).
event.remains: Every planar graph that is not 4-regular. If the subquartic reports are right, what remains is planar graphs of maximum degree 5 or more that are not 4-regular, which is most of the class.

judgement.why: Chang and Sun (GD 2024, refereed LIPIcs) settle the 4-regular class: a case, digested by acceptance into refereed proceedings. Förster et al. treat trees and cacti, for which integer-length plane drawings are elementary; the paper's contribution is grid size with integer coordinates, a stronger/changed question, so variant. Kintali's unconditional content is a lemma and the main theorem is a reduction to unproved conjectures: none. Kemnitz–Harborth's maximal-planar construction is a reduction (subgraphs inherit drawings), so none, not a case. Platonic-graph drawings are finitely many instances. Kintali's AI disclosure names no system and describes verification, gap-finding, prose and unspecified examples; nothing identifies AI-produced mathematics in the result, so none.
judgement.doubts: Chang–Sun slides reportedly claim all max-degree-4 graphs are covered; still a case either way. Kintali's 'some examples were generated by AI' is unspecified; if they fed the lemma it would still be a none-scope event. Pre-snapshot class results (Biedl, Benediktovich) rest on unlocated sources.
